note: Textbook on the physical criteria, outside on the commercial ones. He is emphatically not deconditioned — 5'10" and 174 lb, four to five training days a week, 137 walking miles a month, hikes 4,000-footers, surfs and snowshoes — and good-to-great is close to a perfect description of the ask: 17 consecutive weeks of self-directed progress and an explicit 'How do we get to the next level?'. On neglected_health he passes the severity test the criterion actually applies, since he is not in crisis, though the label reads oddly here because health is the most attended-to thing in his life, not the neglected one. He fails the two criteria that do the qualifying. Occupation is a retired UPS delivery driver of 32 years, which is not 'they own their own business, or they're a physician, something along those lines'. On income he is a retiree on a fixed income by his own unprompted description — 'I'm on a fixed income now' — living on a pension, newly started social security and a 401k, weighing $6,000 against booked travel and a $2,200 surfboard he had just ordered, and declining to quantify any of it. He has capital but no earnings, which is not what the stated criterion tests. Two things this call adds to the standing ICP findings. First, it is a third case of the corpus producing a prospect who fits the programme better than he fits the ICP: nobody in this batch is a more natural kettlebell-longevity client, and the stated criteria would screen him out on occupation and income. Second, it sharpens the existing observation that the ICP carries no clinical criterion — the one screen that genuinely mattered here was cardiac, since this prospect has surgically treated AFib and SVT with residual arrhythmia, and there is no criterion in the stated ICP for it to fail. The stated ICP would reject him for having been a delivery driver and accept him with an untreated arrhythmia.
